headline: German medical cannabis prices fall 22% as patients take on insurers
dek: Medical flower now averages €6 a gram in Germany, while 65,000 patients cut off by insurers face years of litigation before a 20 November Bundesrat debate.
key_points: The average listed price of medical cannabis flower in Germany fell about 22% in a year, to €6.00 a gram, while the number of flower products rose 73% to 2,381, according to Business of Cannabis data.

Statutory health insurers stopped paying for flower on 30 July, cutting off about 65,000 patients; social courts in Frankfurt and Leipzig have backed the insurers, while one in Landshut sided with a patient.
The Federal Constitutional Court refused to hear an individual patient's complaint because lower courts had not been exhausted, leaving a route through the courts that could take years.
The Bundesrat is due to consider the Notfallreform, which softens a rule on trying finished medicines first, on 20 November; it does not restore flower reimbursement.
body: Germany's medical cannabis market is getting bigger and cheaper at the same time, and the people who used to have their flower paid for by health insurers are now fighting for it in court. Two pieces of reporting published by Business of Cannabis in early November show both sides of that squeeze: a price slide across the self-pay market, and a legal stalemate for the patients pushed into it.

Over the year to September 2026, the number of medical flower products listed for sale rose from 1,378 to 2,381, about 73%, while the unweighted average price fell from €7.70 to €6.00 a gram, about 22%. The most common price is now just under €5 a gram. Meanwhile about 65,000 patients who lost statutory insurance coverage for flower on 30 July have found that the fastest legal route back is closed.
## A market built on self-pay

Germany moved cannabis out of its narcotics law in April 2024, and the separate Medical Cannabis Act (MedCanG) made prescribing far easier. Since then, the medical market has grown rapidly on the back of telemedicine. Business of Cannabis puts the market at roughly €1.15 billion, with private self-pay prescriptions making up about 80% to 90% of it. Statutory health insurance, the system that covers most Germans, was always a small slice.

More than 30 online clinics now offer consultations and prescriptions, many with delivery within one or two days. The five largest drew more than 5.7 million combined web visits in September, according to Similarweb data cited in the analysis, though visits are not prescriptions. Clinics compete on discounts and delivery speed, even though the Federal Court of Justice ruled in March that advertising prescription-only cannabis to consumers is not allowed.

With more products chasing the same patients, suppliers are competing on volume rather than premium positioning. Importers have set records quarter after quarter since 2024, according to data from the federal drug regulator BfArM.
## Patients cut off, courts split

The second pressure came from Berlin. A cost-saving law aimed at stabilising insurance contribution rates removed dried flower from statutory reimbursement from 30 July, with no transition period. Extracts, dronabinol and nabilone remain covered, so some patients switched products. Others moved to self-pay, where they meet the falling prices described above.

Patients who sued have had mixed results in emergency proceedings. A social court in Frankfurt ruled on 21 August that removing flower from the law ends the claim outright. A Leipzig court reached the same conclusion on 16 September for a patient reimbursed since 2018, holding that an earlier approval does not survive the new statute; that case is on appeal to the Saxony Higher Social Court. A court in Landshut went the other way, ordering an insurer to keep paying for a dialysis patient while his challenge proceeds. All three rulings are provisional and bind no other court.
> Germany has made cannabis medicine easy to get and hard to get paid for, and the courts now decide which matters more.
## The constitutional shortcut that failed

Patients had hoped for a quicker answer from Karlsruhe. Instead, the Federal Constitutional Court declined to hear an individual's complaint, calling it manifestly inadmissible because the patient was not directly affected in the constitutional sense and had not first gone through the lower courts. A broader complaint is being prepared by the patient association ACM with lawyer Oliver Tolmein but had not been filed when Business of Cannabis reported on it.

That leaves the slow road. A higher social court ruling would bind courts in its own state; a ruling from the Federal Social Court in Kassel would settle the issue nationally, but such cases typically take three to five years or more.
## Margins under pressure

The commercial fallout is already visible. The specialist cannabis pharmacy Lux 99 in Hürth filed for insolvency on 24 October, blaming the insurance changes for removing the reimbursed patients its model depended on. The pharmacy association VCA has warned that price pressure in self-pay is squeezing margins for pharmacies taking on former insured patients.

There is a further risk on the horizon. The Health Ministry has pushed amendments to the MedCanG that would require an in-person consultation before a first prescription and stop mail-order pharmacies from supplying medical cannabis. Their final Bundestag votes have been postponed with no date. Prohibition Partners projects the market could shrink by up to half if they pass.
## The 20 November vote

Lawmakers did soften one part of the insurance package. The Bundestag passed an emergency-care reform, the Notfallreform, on 15 October with twelve amendments to the savings law. One of them narrows a mandatory six-month trial of finished cannabis medicines for new patients, so it now applies only where a licensed finished medicine exists for the condition, with the duration left to the doctor. That largely undercuts a route that would have steered new chronic pain patients towards Vertanical's Exilby, which launched on 1 September at €745.40 a pack.

The Bundesrat is expected to deliberate on 20 November. Because the law does not require the upper chamber's consent, it can object but cannot block it outright. Crucially for the 65,000, the amendment does not restore flower reimbursement.
## What to watch

Watch the Bundesrat on 20 November, the Saxony appeal in the Leipzig case, and whether ACM files its broader constitutional complaint. On the market side, the next price data will show whether the slide below €5 a gram for the most common products continues, and any date for the final MedCanG vote will be the single biggest signal for telemedicine platforms and importers.
